notes.1a: Some candidates found this question challenging with several linking the pulmonary vein to the lungs. A significant number of candidates drew only three lines, one to each box on the right despite the instructions telling them to draw four lines.
notes.1b: The presence or absence of valves was straightforward. The thickness of the walls was more challenging, but both are thinner than the artery walls. Some candidates put not thick, rather than thin.
notes.2ai: This question was well-answered by those candidates who followed the instructions and wrote a word equation. However, those who tried to write a symbol equation often gave symbols for the substances that were incorrect and could not be credited.
notes.2aii: A well-answered question but the emphasis was on the type of energy not the source, so ‘Sun’ was not accepted.
notes.2bi: Most candidates correctly identified a palisade cell although some included the epidermis. Few identified the xylem with many indicating a guard cell or the stoma as the cell conducting water.
notes.2bii: The question asked for a cell structure, but many candidates wrote chlorophyll rather than chloroplast.
notes.2ci: The majority of candidates answered correctly. The commonest error was to give the highest temperature (40 °C) rather than the temperature at which the rate of photosynthesis was highest.
notes.2cii: Most candidates only gained one mark for correctly selecting the correct data from the table (42 and 77) which is the rate at 20 °C and 30 °C. The question asked for three significant figures which some candidates found challenging.
notes.3ai: Generally well-answered but some candidates stated oviduct instead of ovaries.
notes.3aii: Well-answered; those that did not gain full marks mostly omitted to tick both columns for changes in body shape.
notes.3b: The most common error was incorrectly identifying the umbilical cord.
notes.3c: The answers to this question were often too vague and mostly colloquial. Some described fertilisation rather than labour. Typical answers included waters break, contractions start, baby is born, umbilical cord is cut . More detail was needed to score the marks. Candidates mentioned dilation but not in relation to the cervix. References to the vagina were rare although nearly every candidate referred to the presence of a doctor. Several candidates referred to the baby being in the mother’s stomach.
notes.3di: Candidates answered this well. A common error was to state a single weight rather than a range.
notes.3dii: Most candidates were able to select the correct data from the table.
notes.3diii: Few candidates gave the correct answer ‘continuous’, most gave ‘birthweight’.
notes.4ai: Candidates knowledge of this part of the syllabus varied. Those who scored marks usually wrote about filtering and settlement.
notes.4aii: Answers to this question could be general or specific. Candidates usually gave specific answers such as oil or garbage.
notes.4bi: Few candidates could name the molecule that was broken down to make urea.
notes.4bii: Most candidates thought this process took place in the kidney rather than the liver.
notes.4c: Many candidates wrote about plants rather than animals. Pollution was not credited unless qualified by the pollutant.
notes.5a: Mostly well-answered except for the final missing word ‘ventilation’ which was not widely known.
notes.5bi: Several candidates wrote lung or membrane rather than alveolus, possibly due to incorrect reading of the question.
notes.5bii: Although some candidates correctly answered the question, a significant number got the answers the wrong way round.
notes.5biii: Many candidates wrote osmosis which was incorrect as the question asked about molecules so it must be diffusion.
notes.6a: Most candidates were awarded two marks on this question. Those candidates that did not score tended to get confused between the number of smokers or sufferers of chronic bronchitis and the percentage. Some just listed what data was collected rather that what it showed e.g., the percentage of smokers and non-smokers, if they have chronic bronchitis and their age. Few gained a third mark for a correct data quote.
notes.6bi: Candidates usually named one of the cancers and sometimes CHD. A few mentioned COPD.
notes.6ci: The toxic components of tobacco smoke were well-known. Carbon monoxide was often missed, or carbon dioxide was written instead.
notes.7a: Few candidates correctly stated mitosis. There were a wide range of incorrect answers suggesting candidates were unfamiliar with mitosis.
notes.7b: Very few candidates deduced the correct answer from the data. The DNA took 8 hours to double in mass.
notes.7ci: Most candidates identified some of the different structures, almost all identified the nucleus and cell membrane. Few identified the jelly coat or flagellum, often putting tail instead.
notes.7cii: Possible molecules that are energy stores in an egg cell were not well-known. The most common incorrect answer was glucose.
notes.8a: Many candidates were awarded two marks. Biological was an incorrect answer for mechanical and antigens was often confused with antibodies.
notes.8b: This question gave candidates the opportunity to give a wide range of answers. As the question asked about individuals in their homes, answers included personal hygiene, ways of preparing food and waste disposal.
notes.9a: Very few candidates were able to correctly define a sense organ. Most did not mention receptor cells and simply defined an organ or gave examples of sense organs.
notes.9b: Most candidates knew the structure of the eye and the function of the parts of the eye.
notes.9c: The majority of candidates correctly drew the pupil with a smaller diameter.
